abstract: Glycyl radical enzymes (GREs) use a post-translationally installed glycyl radical cofactor to catalyze chemically challenging reactions that are critical for anaerobic metabolism in microorganisms. Despite its importance, the GRE superfamily remains undercharacterized in part due to the vastness of its sequence space. Herein, we use sequence similarity network (SSN) analysis to survey the sequence diversity of the GRE superfamily and identify previously uncharacterized subfamilies. By analyzing the conserved domain architecture of each uncharacterized cluster, we find an unexpected cluster of GRE sequences from diverse photosynthetic eukaryotes. Bioinformatic, biochemical, and structural studies together demonstrate that these GREs have their catalytic subunits fused with a GRE-activating enzyme (GRE-AE). We characterize a highly expressed member of this subfamily as a functional pyruvate formate-lyase that is activated by its fused AE. Low resolution cryogenic electron microscopy confirms that this protein is a naturally occurring fusion, with a central dimeric GRE domain and one GRE-AE domain on each side. We further find that the GRE/GRE-AE fusion proteins are transcriptionally active in a wide range of diatoms and related microalgae. Overall, these findings uncover a previously unappreciated role for GRE-mediated anaerobic metabolism in ecologically important phototrophs, reveal that an attached AE can install a glycyl radical species on its cognate GRE, and show that domain architecture analysis is a powerful strategy to find novel enzymes among large enzyme superfamilies.
